🌏 🌀 Typhoon Fung-wong (2025) — Current System- Alert
https://t.co/IfY6nyw9bU
Now intensifying east of the Philippines with winds near 215 km/h, Typhoon Fung-wong (Uwan) mirrors the paths of past giants.
Infrared imagery shows a perfectly symmetric core and expanding outflow shield — a signature of Category 4 systems.
Rainfall potential already exceeds 350 mm/24 h across Luzon and northern Visayas.
⚡ Historic Typhoons in the Same Corridor
Yolanda (Haiyan, 2013)  |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■| 315 km/h  Catastrophic  
Mangkhut (2018)         |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■   | 285 km/h  Severe  
Meranti (2016)          |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■     | 295 km/h  Major  
Koppu (2015)            |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■                    | 200 km/h  Flooding  
Odette (2021)           |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■               | 240 km/h  Coastal Impact  
Fung-wong (2025)        |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■             | 215 km/h  Ongoing

Each storm shared the same formation zone — the Philippine Sea convergence band between 5° N – 15° N, powered by 30 °C waters and a strong subtropical ridge steering west-northwest.
🌋 Why This Corridor Is So Explosive
Warmest sea surface patch on Earth (≈ 30.5 °C).
Deep ocean heat content amplifies intensification cycles.
The Sierra Madre and Taiwan’s Central Range funnel storm energy northward.
Jet-stream coupling aloft creates massive upper-level ventilation.
Every decade, at least one super-typhoon follows this precise route — a repeating atmospheric pattern now clearly visible from SpaceTracker’s composite storm atlas.
🧠 Scientific Insight
The SpaceTracker Historic Typhoon Atlas aligns data from:
NOAA · JMA · JTWC · Himawari 8 · CIRA
Cross-referenced with high-resolution water-vapour & IR bands to reconstruct storm cores and overlapping historical trajectories (1950–2025).
These overlapping paths reveal a climatological echo — where the next generation of cyclones often emerge within the outflow-cooled wakes of previous ones.
📊 Intensity Comparison Bar
Category 1  |■■■■                                | 120 km/h  
Category 2  |■■■■■■■■                            | 155 km/h  
Category 3  |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■                     | 185 km/h  
Category 4  |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■             | 215 km/h  
Category 5  |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■  | 315 km/h
Peak: Haiyan (2013) — 315 km/h
Current: Fung-wong (2025) — 215 km/h (approaching Cat 4+ threshold)
🌦️ Regional Risk Outlook
Northern Luzon: Torrential rainfall + high wind risk (Saturday–Sunday).
Taiwan East Coast: 6–9 Nov: significant storm surge (1–2 m).
Ryukyu Islands: Peripheral winds 80–100 km/h.
East China Coast: Post-tropical transition expected 11–12 Nov.

💠 Closing Statement

The Western Pacific remains the planet’s most powerful typhoon corridor — a natural engine where heat, humidity, and geography combine with devastating precision.
 Fung-wong (2025) is not just another storm — it’s the next chapter in a 75-year atmospheric pattern that defines life and risk along the Pacific Rim.

#UwanPH
🚨 UPDATE🚨 03:00 8 Nov. 2025  UTC
⚠️ Possible risks include damaging winds, heavy rainfall, storm surge, rough seas, mudslides, and flash flooding.

⚠️Warning Number 16. Information provided by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC).

The combination of heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding will result in Fung-wong/Uwan being a 5 on the AccuWeather RealImpact™ Scale for Tropical Cyclones in the northern Philippines, the strongest rating on the scale.

Typhoon Uwan (international name: Fung-wong) is expected to bring widespread, heavy to torrential rainfall in the northern Philippines, with forecast totals reaching up to 450 mm (18 inches) and an AccuWeather Local StormMax of 900 mm (36 inches). 

The specific rainfall expectations for various regions are:

Northern Philippines (Luzon, Batanes, and Babuyan Islands): Heavy rain is expected from Sunday, November 9, through Tuesday, November 11. Rainfall totals may reach up to 450 mm (18 inches), with a maximum of 900 mm (36 inches) in some areas. This could lead to extensive flooding and mudslides.

Bicol, Quezon, Aurora, Isabela, and most of Northern Luzon: Rains are expected to become "intense" to "torrential" as the typhoon makes landfall, causing widespread flash floods and landslides.

Metro Manila: Heavy to intense rain is anticipated starting Sunday afternoon and continuing into Monday.

AFP Chief of Staff Pays Personal Respects to Fallen Airmen

AFP Chief of Staff General Romeo S Brawner Jr visited the Philippine Air Force (PAF) Mortuary today, November 8, to personally offer condolences to the families of the airmen who tragically perished in an aircraft accident in Agusan del Sur on November 4, 2025. 

During the visit, General Brawner paid his respects to the remains of Captain Paulie B Dumagan PAF and Second Lieutenant Royce Louis G Camigla PAF, two of the six airmen who lost their lives in the line of duty.

The airmen were aboard an aircraft that crashed while providing critical support to communities devastated by Tropical Storm Tino.

Speaking with the grieving families, he expressed the nation’s deep gratitude for the courage and selflessness of their loved ones, who embodied the highest ideals of service and sacrifice.///
